To deface something means to deliberately damage or spoil the way it looks — especially its surface or outward appearance — by marking, scratching, writing, painting, or otherwise messing it up in a way that makes it look ugly, damaged, or difficult to read and recognize.

Think of it this way: the word contains the idea of a face — the visible front of something. To de-face it is to attack or ruin that face.
What Makes Defacing Specific

Defacing is not random destruction. It has three important qualities:

1. It targets appearance, not structure.
When something is defaced, it is not necessarily broken apart or made useless. It is marred — its looks are spoiled. A statue that has been spray-painted with graffiti is still a statue. It is still standing. But it has been defaced.

2. It is almost always deliberate.
People don't accidentally deface things. The act is intentional — someone chose to mark, scratch, or write on something.

3. The thing being defaced usually has value, dignity, or public importance.
You typically hear "deface" used with things that were meant to be respected, preserved, or clearly read — monuments, public buildings, official documents, gravestones, currency, or artworks. This is why defacing carries a strong sense of disrespect and wrongdoing.
What Gets Defaced? (Common Objects)

• Public monuments and statues — perhaps the most classic example. Someone sprays graffiti on a war memorial. That memorial has been defaced.
  • Buildings and walls — painting or scratching unwanted markings onto them.
  • Currency (banknotes and coins) — writing or drawing on paper money. In many countries, this is actually illegal.
  • Official documents — crossing out text, scribbling on them, or altering their content in a way that damages their integrity or readability.
  • Road signs and notices — scratching off letters, spray-painting over them.
  • Gravestones and memorials — damaging the inscriptions or appearance of a tombstone.
  • Artworks and books — drawing on a painting or scribbling across pages of a book.
  • Websites — hackers sometimes "deface" a website by breaking in and replacing its content with unwanted images or messages. This is called website defacement and is the digital equivalent of graffiti.
How Is Defacing Done?

The methods of defacing are as varied as the objects themselves. Common ways include:

  • Spraying paint or graffiti
  • Scratching or carving into a surface
  • Writing or drawing on something with a pen, marker, or chalk
  • Sticking stickers or posters onto something
  • Burning marks into a surface
  • Digitally altering or hacking content online
Important Distinctions

Deface vs. Destroy
These are not the same. To destroy something is to ruin it completely — to break it apart, burn it down, or make it cease to exist. To deface something is gentler in degree. The object survives, but its appearance is damaged. A building that is blown up is destroyed. A building that is spray-painted is defaced.

Deface vs. Vandalize
These two words are close cousins and are often used in similar situations, but they are not identical. Vandalize is a broader word that covers all kinds of deliberate damage to property — smashing windows, breaking furniture, slashing tires. Deface is more specific: it almost always refers to damage done to the surface or appearance of something, especially by marking or writing on it. All defacing can be called vandalism, but not all vandalism is defacing.

Deface vs. Alter
To alter something simply means to change it — and it can be neutral or even positive. To deface it means to change it in a way that damages its appearance or dignity. The negative judgment is built into the word "deface."
The Tone of the Word

"Deface" is a word with a serious, disapproving tone. When you use it, you are communicating that something wrong has been done — that something of value has been disrespected. It appears frequently in news reports, legal language, and formal writing.

It is rarely, if ever, used positively. You would not say an artist "defaced" a canvas when painting a beautiful picture. The word always implies damage, disrespect, or wrongdoing.
Is It Ever Used Metaphorically?

Occasionally, yes. You might see "deface" used to describe something abstract being spoiled — for example, a lie that "defaced" someone's reputation, or poor design choices that "defaced" the beauty of a neighborhood. However, this metaphorical use is much less common than the physical one. In everyday usage, stick to the physical meaning and you will almost always be correct.
The Legal Side

In most countries, defacing public or private property, currency, or official government documents is a criminal offense. The seriousness of the charge depends on what was defaced, how badly, and whether it was motivated by hatred (such as defacing a place of worship or a memorial). Courts and legal documents use the word "deface" frequently in these contexts.
Example Sentences

• Vandals defaced the war memorial with red spray paint overnight.
  • It is illegal to deface currency in most countries.
  • The ancient temple was defaced when tourists carved their names into its walls.
  • Hackers defaced the company's website, replacing its homepage with a political message.
  • The historic statue was defaced beyond recognition before the police arrived.
  • He was charged with defacing public property after authorities reviewed the security footage.
Summary in One Sentence

To deface something is to intentionally damage or spoil its outward appearance — particularly by marking, writing on, or otherwise messing up its surface — in a way that is disrespectful, harmful, and usually illegal.
